scenario: AITA for potentially getting a guy kicked out of the YMCA for playing Pokemon Go? | I (F18) work at a food place that’s placed inside a YMCA. Its in the middle of a long hallway that leads to four hockey arenas and is secluded from the more popular areas of the Y such as the gym. it’s summer, no people except the staff of the Y that aren’t near where my work is. Days are slow therefore I’m booked to work alone. Last saturday I had a shift, and no one was there except the casual gym nuts that ordering from my store. One man, mid 30s was one of my customers that day. I didn’t make much of it at first, he ordered some food from me and then that was that, a normal customer transaction. However, i noticed how he walked back and forth every few minutes in the hallway between my store and the arenas that lead to the gym. I really didn’t care at this point, and went onto minding my business. He continues to do so for three hours of my shift and I start freaking out, but i end up not doing anything except panic silently until the next person takes my shift. Monday rolls by and I had a closing shift alone. 3 hours left of my shift the same guy comes back. He bought more food and this time i asked if he worked in the facility, and replied “no, i’m just visiting.” I felt uneasy about the whole interaction given what happened, but he left with his food right away and i took a breath of relief. However, 30 minutes later I see him once more pace the same path he took saturday, this time looking at his phone then into the store and everytime He does this for another 2 hours and I continue to do my usual work routine, but now with shaky hands, avoiding eye contact with this creep. I don’t deal really well with confrontations due to my anxiety so i quietly suffered in my nervous sweat alone. Thankfully my parents came to visit knowing I had a night shift. told them what was going on and was going on and was comforted. Since I had to start closing my mom went to go get the security for me to talk to, and dad stood guard while i cleaned the store. the staff gave me phone numbers and said they’d escort me if ever I felt unsafe. They also said that they’ve checked the cameras and even got the guy’s face and the next time he does this will be kicked out, doesn’t matter if its me who saw. The staff and I never confronted the guy but he continued to pace back and forth while i was talking to the staff and he ended up leaving since the place was closing for the night. Once home, my dad told me that everytime the guy passed by he would give him the dirty look while we were talking to the YMCA staff. The man then told my dad that he was just playing Pokemon Go and even showed him his phone. I now feel like an asshole if this were to be true, but doesn’t stop the fact that if he really was just playing a game, the next time he’s going to do it he’ll face be kicked out of the YMCA. AITA?

Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!)
